sections.title: An organ, a cell and a signal
paragraphs: An ovary, an egg and estrogen all belong in an explanation of reproduction. But they do different jobs. If we treat the three names as interchangeable, we lose the connection between the structure that produces something and the product that leaves it.

A gonad is a reproductive organ that produces gametes and releases reproductive hormones. The testes are the male gonads, and the ovaries are the female gonads. A gamete is a reproductive cell: a sperm or an egg. A hormone is a chemical messenger. Testosterone, estrogen and progesterone are examples of reproductive hormones.

Consider a testis. Sperm develop in tiny tubes within the organ, while other cells release testosterone into the blood. The sperm can travel through reproductive ducts. Testosterone travels in the blood to tissues able to respond to it. One organ contributes both a cell and a signal, but those products have different routes and functions.

A human gamete normally carries one set of 23 chromosomes. At fertilization, a sperm and an egg contribute one set each, so the resulting cell has 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes. The gonad does not leave the parent and join another gonad. The cells it helps produce carry the chromosome contributions. The details of chromosome separation will come with meiosis.

sections.title: What makes a characteristic primary or secondary?
paragraphs: Primary sex characteristics are the reproductive organs and structures themselves. Testes, ovaries, reproductive ducts, the uterus, penis and vagina belong in this category. Most of these structures are present at birth and continue to develop. Primary names a biological category; it does not mean more important.

Secondary sex characteristics are other physical features associated with sexual maturation. Examples include facial-hair growth, a deeper voice and breast development. They become more noticeable as hormone activity changes during puberty. The examples describe patterns with considerable variation among people, rather than a checklist everyone must match.

Now compare an ovary becoming more active with breast development. Both can change during puberty. The ovary remains a reproductive organ, so it remains a primary characteristic. Breast development belongs to the secondary category used here. The timing is similar; the kind of structure or feature is different. That is why the observation 'it changed at puberty' cannot settle the classification by itself.

A reproductive duct is also primary even though it does not make gametes. An oviduct, for example, helps transport the egg toward the uterus. Primary characteristics include structures that support transport and other reproductive functions, not just the gonads.

sections.title: How a chromosome signal reaches a developing tissue
paragraphs: In the typical chromosome patterns considered here, XX is associated with female reproductive development and XY with male reproductive development. X and Y are called sex chromosomes. These chromosome combinations are established at fertilization, before the reproductive organs have taken their later form. The chromosome pattern and the developed anatomy describe different parts of the explanation.

A gene is a stretch of DNA containing information used by cells. SRY is a gene usually carried on the Y chromosome. Its activity helps initiate testis development. Hormones from the developing testes, including testosterone, then contribute to the development of reproductive tissues. The sequence links genetic information, an organ that develops, and signals produced by that organ. Testosterone alone does not explain every reproductive structure.

A hormone produces its usual effect only when a target cell can respond. A receptor is a molecule in or on a cell that recognises a particular signal. A hormone can be present in the blood while a tissue lacking a functioning receptor has a reduced or absent response to it. Measuring the signal therefore does not tell us everything about the tissue's response.

The XX/XY account is a model of typical development. Variations in genes, hormone production and tissue responses also occur. Use the stated model when explaining the biology, and keep conclusions within its information. These anatomy categories do not determine a person's identity.

sections.title: Puberty brings existing structures into new activity
paragraphs: Puberty is a period of increased reproductive hormone activity and developing reproductive capacity. The hypothalamus, a region of the brain, and the anterior pituitary, a hormone-releasing gland below it, help coordinate signals to the gonads. The reproductive organs develop further, gamete-related activity changes, and secondary characteristics become more apparent.

These changes connect the ideas we have separated. A gonad is the organ; a gamete is a reproductive cell; a hormone is a signal. A primary structure can become more active at puberty without changing category. A secondary feature is classified by what it is, rather than just when it appeared.

When you explain a new observation, name the structure or product first. Then follow its route and describe its effect. We will use that approach to follow sperm from their production site through the male reproductive ducts.

worked.title: A hormone is present, but one tissue responds differently
worked.scenario: In a stated classroom model, two tissues receive the same reproductive hormone from the blood. Tissue A has functioning receptors for it. Tissue B lacks functioning receptors for it. Other conditions needed for the response are the same. Does the shared hormone supply establish that both tissues respond normally?
steps: Identify what is shared: both tissues receive the chemical signal. This information concerns hormone delivery, not the production of gametes or the presence of a gonad.

Identify what differs: the tissues' receptors. A functioning receptor allows the target cell to recognise the signal. Tissue A can make the usual response under the stated conditions. Tissue B's response will be reduced or absent.

Check the proposed conclusion against both requirements. Delivery is present in both tissues, but the ability to respond is not. The same hormone supply is therefore insufficient to establish the same response.
Keep the conclusion bounded. This model changes a receptor condition. It does not tell us that Tissue B changed its chromosome number or that the hormone became a sperm or egg.

optional.question: A description names a uterus, an egg and progesterone. Which is a reproductive organ, which is a gamete, and which is a hormone? Is every reproductive organ a gonad? Explain the distinction before checking.
optional.answer: The uterus is a reproductive organ, the egg is a gamete and progesterone is a hormone. A gonad specifically produces gametes and reproductive hormones. The uterus supports development but is not an ovary or testis and does not produce gametes. The word reproductive therefore describes a wider group of organs than the word gonad.

sections.title: Locate production before tracing the journey
paragraphs: A sperm cell must be produced, mature and travel out of the body. Those jobs happen in connected structures. We will follow the connections rather than make a route out of every nearby label in an anatomy picture.

The two testes lie in the scrotum, a pouch outside the main body cavity. Sperm production works best a little below core body temperature. Moving the testes closer to the body in cold conditions helps retain heat; holding them farther away in warmer conditions helps lose heat. The scrotum helps provide suitable conditions for the organs inside it.

Within each testis, tightly coiled seminiferous tubules are the sperm-production sites. Sperm pass from them through small connecting ducts into the epididymis, a long coiled duct alongside the testis. In the epididymis, sperm mature, acquire the capacity for movement and can be stored. Production and maturation are connected stages at different locations.

Look at the lower part of the side-view diagram. The testis is the oval organ inside the scrotum. Follow the epididymis label to the curved structure along the testis, then find the ductus deferens leaving this region. The black lines connect names to structures; they are label lines, not arrows showing sperm movement. The picture shows a cut-away side view and does not display every small internal duct or the coiled seminiferous tubules.

sections.title: Follow the connected ducts
paragraphs: During ejaculation, coordinated muscular contractions move sperm from the epididymis into the vas deferens. Ductus deferens is another name for this same duct. It carries sperm upward from the testis region and into the pelvis.

At the next junction, the vas deferens joins the duct of a seminal vesicle. The resulting ejaculatory duct carries the mixture through the prostate into the urethra. The urethra then runs through the penis to the outside. The penis is the organ containing that final passage, rather than an extra sperm-producing site. During intercourse, it can deposit semen in the female reproductive tract.

Return to the figure. Trace the labelled ductus deferens upward and around the bladder region, then locate the short ejaculatory duct near the seminal vesicle and prostate. Find the urethra continuing through the penis. The path passes near the urinary bladder; it does not go through the bladder's storage space.

The male urethra is shared by the urinary and reproductive systems, but urine and semen are normally released at different times. The ureter is a different tube: it brings urine to the bladder. Similar names and neighbouring positions do not make the ureter part of the sperm pathway. For the main reproductive route, keep the sequence seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra.

sections.title: Why the travelling mixture is called semen
paragraphs: Sperm are cells. Semen is the mixture containing sperm and fluid from accessory glands. Accessory means that the glands contribute to the reproductive system without being the gonads that produce the sperm. A gland releases a secretion; a transport duct carries material along a passage.

The seminal vesicles add fructose-containing fluid. Fructose is a sugar that sperm can use as an energy source. The prostate contributes fluid to semen through ducts entering the urethral region. The bulbourethral glands, also called Cowper's glands, release lubricating mucus into the urethra. The combined secretions support sperm activity and help provide a suitable fluid environment, including buffering acidity. A buffer helps resist changes in acidity.

Use the diagram to separate the gland bodies from the route. The seminal vesicle lies behind the bladder, the prostate lies below it around the beginning of the urethra, and Cowper's gland is shown lower down. Secretions reach the route through gland ducts. A sperm does not have to travel through the interior of every gland to receive the fluid it adds.

A fluid sample and a cell sample tell us different things. Seeing fluid leave a gland would establish secretion, not sperm production. Finding sperm in the travelling mixture would identify cells that originated in seminiferous tubules. The name semen describes the combined material and does not make every component come from one structure.

sections.title: Keep the cell route and hormone route separate
paragraphs: The testes also contain interstitial cells, also called Leydig cells, between the seminiferous tubules. These cells release testosterone into the blood. This is an endocrine route: a hormone enters the circulation and reaches responsive tissues. Sperm instead travel through the reproductive duct system. The same organ contributes to both routes, but the routes are physically different.

A useful explanation follows the affected function. A change to a production site first concerns cell production. A change to an epididymis can affect maturation or storage. A change to a transport duct concerns passage along that route. A change in a gland's secretion concerns a fluid contribution. After identifying the first effect, trace which downstream parts depend on it and which still have their own functioning sources.

For an illustration with two testes and paired ducts, check whether a question describes one side or both before claiming that all sperm transport is interrupted. These classroom cases isolate a mechanism; they do not give enough information to diagnose a person's fertility.

We can now connect the journey to the starting question. Seminiferous tubules supply sperm, the epididymis supports maturation, ducts transport them, and accessory glands add fluid. Next, a closer view inside a testis will let us distinguish the cells that become sperm from the cells that support them.

worked.title: A changed gland secretion with an open sperm route
worked.scenario: In a simplified model, sperm production and maturation continue normally and all transport ducts remain open. Only the seminal vesicles' fructose contribution is reduced. What changes directly, and what cannot be concluded from that change alone?
steps: Locate the changed source. The seminal vesicles are accessory glands. They contribute fructose-containing fluid rather than producing the sperm cells.
Follow that contribution into the mixture. Less fructose from these glands reduces an energy-source contribution available to sperm in the seminal fluid. It may affect support for sperm activity.

Check the unchanged conditions. The problem explicitly keeps sperm production, maturation and duct transport functioning. It therefore does not establish that no sperm can enter the mixture or that the urethra is blocked.
Separate the other route as well. Testosterone enters blood from interstitial cells. A changed fructose contribution does not itself show that testosterone release stopped.

Conclude at the level the evidence supports: the gland contribution has changed. The model supplies no measurements that would let us calculate sperm speed, an exact sperm count or a probability of fertilization.

optional.question: In a second model, both testes still produce sperm but passage through both epididymides is completely interrupted. Accessory glands and their downstream ducts remain open. Explain which material loses its route and whether gland fluid must also disappear. Then identify one difference from the worked gland-secretion example.
optional.answer: Newly produced sperm cannot pass through the interrupted epididymides to reach the downstream sperm ducts. Accessory-gland fluid still has its own downstream entry points, so it need not disappear. This prediction concerns new transport after the interruption; it does not determine whether sperm were already stored farther along before it occurred. Unlike the worked example, this model changes a cell-transport route rather than only the composition of a gland secretion.
